headline: WWE’s Jermaine Haley, known as Bronson Reed, dies of medical complications
author: Dhruti Shah

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Reporter covering international breaking news
Jermaine Haley, whom World Wrestling Entertainment fans knew as Bronson Reed, has died of medical complications at 38.
WWE confirmed in a statement that Mr. Haley had died on Friday. It did not give further information on the cause of his death.

The company said its thoughts were with Mr. Haley’s pregnant wife, Paige, and the couple’s daughter, adding: “Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague.”

WWE remembers the legacy of Jermaine Haley, also known as Bronson Reed. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jermaine’s entire family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter, as well as his friends, co-workers and fans. pic.twitter.com/SZNt4GEVLE— WWE (@WWE) November 28, 2026
Tributes were paid and a 10-bell salute in honor of Mr. Haley was held during a WWE event in Akins Ford Arena in Athens, Georgia, on Friday.
Online, Grayson Waller thanked the fellow Australian (Mr. Haley was born in Adelaide) for “opening so many doors for myself and many others in Australian wrestling.”
Mr. Haley joined WWE in 2019 and had two stints there. A former NXT North American champion, he also won the Andre the Giant Memorial Battle Royal in 2024.
Mr. Haley’s last appearance was at the WWE Crown Jewel in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Nov. 7.
Initial tests show no lead in drinking water near Iowa detonation site, EPA says

The Environmental Protection Agency says preliminary tests indicate the controlled detonation that took place in Middleton, Iowa, on Wednesday did not lead to an increase in lead levels in sources of drinking water in the surrounding area.

The Army detonated nearly 10,000 pounds of degrading lead explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunitions Plant, saying this was necessary because the stockpile of lead azide had become so unstable it feared it would spontaneously explode.
The operation was postponed several times amid a legal challenge and outcry from residents and local officials who feared the blast would create a plume of toxic lead dust.

The EPA said Saturday it “found no lead in the 38 water samples taken post-detonation at public water supplies, which included samples of finished treated drinking water and untreated water at the intake.”
It added that it had also monitored air quality for 30 consecutive hours after the detonation and detected no airborne lead.
The agency is still processing tap water, soil, dust and air samples, and says results will be posted online.
Activists in Iowa have said public pushback to the Army’s original proposal had made the explosion safer and more transparent, The Post reported.
Reporter covering politics and breaking news
What it was like to keep a 410-person band in NYC for the rescheduled Macy’s parade

After Macy’s said it would postpone its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade until Saturday because of inclement weather, performing groups from around the country scrambled to decide whether to extend their stays in New York City or head home without marching down to 34th Street.

For the marching band at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, known as the Marching Illini, the decision to stay “was pretty unanimous,” band director Barry L. Houser said. The logistics of keeping hundreds of band members in Manhattan for two extra days were a challenge, he said, but “everyone’s just been phenomenal.”

First, Houser said, the band had to weigh whether to stay or head back to Illinois to give students time to prepare for their final full week of classes this semester. Then they had to ensure that hotel rooms were available and that they had enough money to extend the trip. The band travels with 436 people, including 410 student performers, Houser said.
Their hotel had room for the whole group to stay, Houser said, but there was a catch: Everyone had to check out and then check back in.
“Adding instruments to that mix in a hotel lobby that is not designed for 436 people — we’ve had to make some accommodations there,” Houser said.
Catering changes and charter bus rescheduling soon fell in line, and the band was able to fundraise more than $175,000 to pay for their extended stay, Houser said.
The Marching Illini’s parade set is poised to include a custom arrangement of “Chicago” by Sufjan Stevens. Video from the band’s rehearsal of the piece went viral this week.
On Sunday, the band will board buses for the long drive back to Champaign, just in time for their last full week of classes.
The trip to Manhattan from Illinois, Houser said, was about 19 hours long.
Data reporter focusing on climate and the environment
Where high tides set records on both coasts this week
Oceans raged along the Pacific and Atlantic coasts of the U.S. this week as a combination of king tides, strong swells and a winter storm sent water levels into record territory.

Along the Mid-Atlantic coast, a winter storm that brought 60 mph to 70 mph winds and waves up to 20 feet coincided with some of the highest tides of the year to send ocean waters rushing into communities along the coast.
“Everything was in the right place for a worst-case scenario,” said Larry Brown, a meteorologist in the National Weather Service’s Wakefield, Virginia, office.

Waters surged 1.5 feet beyond the prior record at the tide station at Wachapreague, Virginia, according to preliminary data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The previous record was set during Tropical Storm Ernesto in 2006, and the station dates back to 1978.

Along the California coast, a record El Niño has caused warmer-than-usual waters to accumulate, raising sea levels by more than a foot in some areas. When king tides arrived earlier this week they were accompanied by a strong ocean swell that generated 20-foot to 30-foot waves. The combination sent waves over roads and into homes and businesses, and caused part of a pier to collapse.
Tides set records at stations from San Diego to Monterey, and more intense king tides are expected in December and January.
National correspondent covering Texas, Oklahoma and Louisiana, with expertise in red states
GOP governors invite Texans to move to their states to flee blue wave
HOUSTON — Republican governors have a message for conservative Texans upset by Democrats sweeping every statewide office: “Texit” and move here!
Sen. Tommy Tuberville, Alabama’s governor-elect, tweeted this week, telling any “red-blooded patriot or business wanting to flee the woke-show that is coming to Texas … Alabama is open for business.”
Not to be outdone, Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry then posted a photo of new billboards he erected in Texas saying: “If you’re from Louisiana, it’s time to come home!”
“Louisiana is leading the nation in economic opportunity,” Landry wrote. “Come home and fill these new job opportunities!”
Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt then urged conservative Texans to defect across the northern state line.

“Hey Texans, Oklahoma is open for business, committed to conservative values, and ready to welcome families and entrepreneurs,” Stitt said in a post on X. “Come build your American Dream in Oklahoma!”
Texans — Democrat and Republican alike — had thoughts.
Rep. Joaquin Castro, who as a Texas state lawmaker in 2003 fled to Oklahoma with other Democrats to block Republican congressional redistricting, called Stitt’s invitation “thoughtful” and “kind.”
“I can attest the state was incredibly welcoming,” he said.

Those who rejected the GOP pitch noted that Texas has no state income tax and leads the country in gross domestic product growth and job creation. Others responded with links to Facebook groups offering help to conservative Texans who want to relocate.
“We Texans should all consider Florida or Tennessee now, too,” one retiree in the Houston suburbs posted.
Reporter covering local transportation
Maryland bridge closure alert mistakenly sent callers to sex hotline
People seeking information about a Maryland bridge closure amid Thursday’s storm were in for a surprise: They were mistakenly directed to a sex hotline.
The Maryland Department of Emergency Management sent residents a public safety alert Thursday afternoon warning that the strong Thanksgiving storm had closed the Chesapeake Bay Bridge.
That alert mistakenly directed callers to a sex hotline rather than the Maryland Transportation Authority, or MDTA.

In a statement, Maryland Transportation Authority spokesman Brad Tanner said the authority was “aware of the unfortunate error” included in the emergency alert’s callback number. The agency has corrected the error, Tanner said in the statement.
“We know this was distressing to many Marylanders,” Tanner said. “Emergency alerts are critical, lifesaving tools that require accuracy, and the MDTA takes this error very seriously.”
Thursday’s storm, the worst to hit on Thanksgiving Day in decades, left hundreds of thousands of people without power up and down the East Coast.
The roughly 4.3-mile-long Bay Bridge is notorious for not having shoulders. Some people are so scared of crossing it that they pay other drivers to take them.
This month, the MDTA said plans to replace the bridge are moving forward after securing final federal environmental approval. Construction is expected to begin as soon as 2032, the agency said.
A Denver man is trapping and egging Waymo’s self-driving cars, police say
The Waymo eggings follow a pattern, Denver police say.

First, the middle-aged man parks his silver Toyota Corolla in front of one of the self-driving cars, stopping the vehicle from moving, a police report says. Then, police say, the man takes orange road cones out of his trunk and places them in front of the Waymo so it can’t move.
The man often then pelts the robotic car with eggs and drives away, leaving the Waymo trapped, the police report says.
An investigator working for Waymo told police the company has recorded 30 incidents of a bearded, ponytailed man trapping and egging its vehicles.

Matt Jablow, a spokesperson for the Denver District Attorney’s Office, said in a statement that his office would work with the city attorney’s office “to identify the most appropriate legal mechanism to make this behavior stop.”

Since Waymo launched in Denver in September 2025, the vehicles have driven past barricades into a farmers market, come close to driving over a freshly paved road and received a parking ticket, local television station 9News reported.
But Mayor Mike Johnston said this week that Waymo cars are mostly working well in Denver.
“They’re popular, energy-friendly, efficient, and affordable,” he said in a statement. “There have been a few expected hiccups here and there, but overall they’re a good egg.”
